summary: This standards-track document defines how to represent and maintain MIXER conformant global address mappings (MCGAMs) in an X.500 or LDAP directory.

plainLanguage.summary: Keeping address translation notes in a directory instead of scattered about.

questions: how are x400 addresses mapped to rfc 822
how does ldap store address mappings
subtitle: How to keep the X.400 to RFC 822 address translation tables in an X.500 or LDAP directory.

tldr.problem: MIXER gateways translate addresses between X.400 and RFC 822 mail, and every gateway needs the same, widely available mapping tables.
tldr.mechanism: The mappings (MCGAMs) are stored in two subtrees of an X.500 or LDAP directory, one per direction, using new object classes and attributes that point to the mapped domain, OR address or gateway.
tldr.outcome: Gateways can share and replicate the tables and look up a mapping in two directory lookups. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1838 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 2164 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1838, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: MCGAMs in a Directory
sections.content:
MIXER (RFC 2156) defines an algorithm that uses a set of global mappings between X.400 and RFC 822 addresses. This RFC defines how to represent and maintain those mappings, called MIXER Conformant Global Address Mappings (MCGAMs), in an X.500 or LDAP directory.

The mappings are global, and a MIXER gateway may use any set of them. The key use of the directory is to let gateways share MCGAMs and share the effort of maintaining and publishing them. Because there is no single place where all MCGAMs are published, the specification allows several sets, each published under one part of the directory.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail systems that speak different languages need a translation list. This document says where to store that list so many post offices can share it.

sections.title: Two Subtrees
sections.content:
Using techniques from RFC 1836 and RFC 2247 for representing OR Address and domain hierarchies in the directory tree, the RFC defines two independent subtrees holding four mappings. They sit under any part of the tree; the examples use OU=MIXER MCGAMs, O=Zydeco Plc, C=GB. The subtree roots use the subtree mechanism from RFC 1837.

  • X.400 to RFC 822: an OR Address tree under CN=X.400 to RFC 822.
  • RFC 822 to X.400: a domain tree under CN=RFC 822 to X.400, which also holds the gateway mapping.

The stated benefits are that the information sits in one clearly defined area that can be widely replicated, that migration from a table-based approach is easier, and that missing components are handled naturally. The RFC mentions and rejects an alternative of putting the data in the routing subtrees, because the chosen approach has greater benefits.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory has two big address books. One turns the old-style addresses into internet-style ones, and the other goes the other way.

sections.title: Object Classes and Omitted Components
sections.content:
Two new object classes carry the mapping values. x400ToRFC822Mapping may contain associatedDomain and associatedInternetGateway. rFC822ToX400Mapping is a subclass of domain-component and may contain associatedORAddress and associatedX400Gateway. The objects give pointers to the mapped components.

MIXER allows omitted components in OR Addresses on either side of a mapping. The omittedORAddressComponent object class, with a required oRAddressComponentType attribute, represents them. The attribute holds the X.500 attribute type of the omitted component, and the mechanism is only for the X.400 to RFC 822 subtree and for the associatedORAddress attribute.

An appendix assigns object identifiers under mhs-ds 4, with object classes at oc 1 to 4 and attributes at at 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry in the address book has a few special boxes that say where the translated address is. There is also a way to mark a part of an address as left out.

sections.title: Mapping from X.400 to RFC 822
sections.content:
An OR Address such as P=Isode; A=Mailnet; C=FI is keyed by a directory entry whose name is built from the address, under the X.400 to RFC 822 subtree. The associatedDomain attribute of that entry gives the domain it maps to. This attribute defines authoritative mappings, which go in the open community tree, and the manager of an MCGAM makes the entry.

The gateway mapping from MIXER is provided by associatedInternetGateway, which may name several gateways. It acts as a fallback if there is no equivalence mapping. An OR Address maps to either a gateway or a domain, so an entry must never hold both attributes.

The longest match is found in three steps: derive a directory name from the OR Address as far as the lowest OU, look it up in the subtree (a failed lookup indicates the longest possible match, which can then be looked up), and check the matched entry for associatedDomain or associatedInternetGateway. The mapping can always be done with two lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: To translate an old-style address you look up its name in the first address book. The entry tells you the matching internet name, or a post office that can take care of it.

sections.title: Mapping from RFC 822 to X.400
sections.content:
The reverse structure follows RFC 1279 for the domain hierarchy. The domain ISODE.COM is represented as DomainComponent=ISODE, DomainComponent=COM, CN=RFC 822 to X.400 under the MCGAM location. Its associatedORAddress attribute, encoded as a distinguished name, holds the mapped OR Address, such as PRMD=Isode, ADMD=Mailnet, C=FI.

The associatedX400Gateway attribute provides the X.400 gateway mapping and may name multiple gateways. As in the other direction, an entry never holds both an associatedX400Gateway and an associatedORAddress. If a gateway is found, the address is encoded as a domain defined attribute relative to the OR Address named by the attribute. If several gateways are found, the MTA may choose whichever it wants.

The lookup derives a directory name from the domain part of the address and looks it up in the subtree. A failure indicates the longest match, which can then be looked up, so two lookups always suffice. Aliases can simplify some table mappings, and the directory can support mapping from addresses that use numeric country codes.
sections.plainLanguage: Going the other way, you look up the internet domain in the second address book. It points to the old-style address, or to a post office that handles that domain.

sections.title: Gateway Selection of MCGAMs
sections.content:
A MIXER gateway names an ordered list of MCGAM collections it will use for lookups. This is held in the mcgamTables attribute, a sequence of distinguished names, on the mixerGateway auxiliary object class, which is a subclass of mhs-message-transfer-agent.

A gateway is not required to use any MCGAMs. When MCGAMs are accessed from multiple sources, the RFC recommends accessing all of the sources to find the one that gives the best match.
sections.plainLanguage: Each post office keeps a short list of which address books it trusts. If it uses several, it should check them all and take the best answer.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The directory directs the translation between X.400 and Internet mail addresses, so it can indirectly affect how messages are routed across a gateway. A successful attack could cause incorrect translation of an originator address, which would forge it, or of a recipient address, which could send mail to an unauthorized recipient or make an authorized recipient think a message was meant for other recipients.

When cryptographic authentication is available for directory responses, clients shall use those mechanisms to verify the authenticity and integrity of the responses.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone tampered with the address book, mail could go to the wrong person. So when the directory can prove its answers are genuine, you must check that proof.
